lessons.title: Sources of Wisdom and Forms of Expression in Christianity
lessons.description: Bible authority, denominations, women's leadership, and Christian art, literature and music.
lessons.content_html:
The Bible as a Source of Wisdom and Authority

The Bible is the foundational source of wisdom and authority for all Christians. The Old Testament contains law, history, the prophets and the writings (Psalms, Proverbs, etc.). The New Testament contains the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, the letters (Epistles) and Revelation. Together these 66 books (Protestant canon) or 73 books (Catholic canon, including the Deuterocanonical/Apocrypha books) form Christian scripture.

Christians interpret the Bible’s authority in different ways. The literal Word of God: some Christians (particularly conservative evangelicals and fundamentalists) hold that every word of the Bible is directly and literally the Word of God, without error. This view takes Genesis 1 as a historical account and reads all biblical commands as binding today. The inspired Word of God: most mainstream Christians believe the Bible is God’s inspired Word, written by human authors under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. It is authoritative in all matters of faith and life, but must be read in its historical and literary context. Source of guidance and teaching: some Christians emphasise that the Bible’s authority lies in its spiritual wisdom and moral teaching rather than in every factual statement. 2 Timothy 3:16 is the key text: “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness.” Dei Verbum (Vatican II, 1965) expresses the Catholic position: Scripture and Tradition together form the single sacred deposit of the Word of God.

Key Fact

For the 5-mark source question, 2 Timothy 3:16 (“All Scripture is God-breathed”) is a reliable and named source of authority that earns the 5th mark when used to support a point about biblical authority. Dei Verbum (Second Vatican Council, 1965) is the Catholic named source. The Book of Common Prayer (Anglican) is a named source of wisdom for how the Bible is used in formal worship. Catechism of the Catholic Church 1777 is a named source for the role of personal conscience in ethical decision-making alongside scripture.

Denominations: The Development of the Church

The Christian Church today is divided into thousands of denominations. Three major streams are most important for this course: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant. The Great Schism of 1054 divided Western Christianity (Catholic, led by the Pope in Rome) from Eastern Christianity (Orthodox, based in Constantinople). The Reformation of the 16th century saw Martin Luther (95 Theses, 1517), John Calvin and others break from Rome over issues of biblical authority (sola scriptura), salvation (sola fide) and the sacraments. Protestant denominations that emerged include Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Methodist, Baptist and Pentecostal/Charismatic churches.

The Filioque clause was a key theological cause of the 1054 Great Schism. The original Nicene Creed (381 AD) states that the Holy Spirit “proceeds from the Father.” Western (Latin) churches gradually added “and the Son” (filioque) without an Ecumenical Council, which the Eastern churches argued was an unauthorised alteration to a Creed binding on the whole Church. The theological dispute: Eastern theology insists that the Father alone is the source of the Trinity (monarchia of the Father); Western theology argues that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son together as one principle. The split between Catholic and Orthodox remains formally unresolved today. Protestant churches inherited the Western (Filioque-inclusive) Nicene Creed. The Church as the Body of Christ (Romans 12:4–6; 1 Corinthians 12) is a key image that all denominations share despite their differences — one body, many members.

Leadership and the Role of Women

Christian churches have diverse leadership structures. Laity are ordinary church members (not ordained). Ministers (also called priests, vicars or pastors depending on denomination) lead congregations. Bishops oversee groups of churches (dioceses). The Pope is the leader of the Roman Catholic Church, believed by Catholics to be the successor of St Peter with universal jurisdiction. Ephesians 4:11–12 describes the purpose of church leadership: “to equip his people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up.” Leaders in all denominations are expected to equip and serve their congregations, not simply to hold authority.

The role of women is a significant point of divergence. Two key passages in Paul’s letters create tension: 1 Corinthians 14:33–40 has been interpreted as restricting women from speaking in church, while Romans 16:1–16 greets Phoebe as a diakonos (deacon or minister), Priscilla as a co-worker, and Junia as “outstanding among the apostles.” These passages together show that women held significant roles in the early Church, while Paul also issued context-specific restrictions. Denominations have reached different conclusions: the Church of England ordained women as priests in 1994 and as bishops from 2015; the Methodist Church has had women ministers since 1974; the Roman Catholic Church and most Orthodox churches do not ordain women to the priesthood.

Arguments for women’s ordination: Galatians 3:28 (not named in the spec but widely cited) states “there is neither male nor female … you are all one in Christ Jesus” — suggesting the Gospel breaks down gender hierarchies. Romans 16:1–16 shows women in leadership in the early Church. The cultural context of 1 Corinthians 14 (specific problems in the Corinthian church) means the passage cannot be applied universally. The Church of England and many Protestant denominations have now ordained women at all levels. Arguments against women’s ordination: The Catholic Church teaches that Christ chose twelve male apostles and the Church has no authority to change this. 1 Corinthians 14:34 is read as a timeless principle of male headship in the Church. Some evangelical Protestants agree that gender roles in the Church are created-order structures, not cultural preferences. In a 12-mark Discuss, students should note that this is a live intra-Christian debate, not just a conservative/progressive binary.

Forms of Expression: Art, Drama, Literature and Music

Christians express their faith through a rich variety of art forms. Paintings and icons: famous examples include Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel ceiling (The Creation of Adam, c.1508–1512) and Rembrandt’s The Return of the Prodigal Son (c.1669). The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2502 says “sacred art is true and beautiful when its form corresponds to its particular vocation: evoking and glorifying, in faith and adoration, the transcendent mystery of God.” Icons are sacred images used especially in Orthodox Christianity as “windows into heaven” — they are not worshipped but venerated as aids to prayer. Many Protestant churches reject icons and statues as potentially idolatrous, while Catholic churches use sculpture and statues of Jesus, Mary and the saints.

Christian symbolism communicates belief without words. The Cross is the primary symbol of Christianity — Ephesians 2:10–19 speaks of Christ reconciling Jew and Gentile through the cross, “destroying the barrier, the dividing wall of hostility.” The fish (ichthus) was an early Christian secret symbol: the Greek letters of the word “fish” form the acronym “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour.” The symbols of the four evangelists (Matthew = man/angel, Mark = lion, Luke = ox, John = eagle) decorate churches and manuscripts worldwide.

Christian drama includes mystery plays (medieval performances of Bible stories) and passion plays (re-enactments of the Passion of Christ, Matthew 26–28). The Oberammergau Passion Play (Bavaria) is performed every ten years and draws pilgrims from around the world. Drama brings the Gospel to life for those who might not read the Bible.

Key Fact

CS Lewis (1898–1963) is the spec-named author for Christian literature. His fiction includes The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950) — an allegory in which the lion Aslan sacrifices himself and returns to life, echoing the death and resurrection of Christ. The Great Divorce (1945) is an allegorical exploration of heaven and hell, presenting heaven as the “solid” reality and earthly life as shadowy in comparison. Lewis is also known for non-fiction Christian apologetics in Mere Christianity (1952). In worship, Gregorian Chant (plainchant dating from the early medieval period) is traditional Catholic and monastic music. Contemporary worship music includes the songs of Graham Kendrick (UK songwriter, including “Shine, Jesus, Shine”) and the American worship band Casting Crowns, whose songs use accessible language to address faith, doubt and identity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers Sections 3 and 4 of the spec — Sources of Wisdom and Forms of Expression. Both sections appear as (c) and (d) questions in your exam. For a 5-mark source question on biblical authority, the two best named sources are 2 Timothy 3:16 (“All Scripture is God-breathed”) and Dei Verbum (Vatican II, 1965). For the role of women, named passages 1 Corinthians 14:33–40 and Romans 16:1–16 are in the spec — use both to show the internal tension. For forms of expression questions, you need to know at least two named works of art, two named authors or composers: CS Lewis (The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe), Gregorian Chant, Graham Kendrick, Casting Crowns. The most common error on 12-mark Discuss questions about women’s ordination or art in worship is presenting only one side — develop the traditional view (no ordination; art as potential idolatry) with genuine theological arguments, not just the “obvious wrong answer.” SPaG: ‘denomination’, ‘conscience’, ‘Reformation’, ‘Filioque’ should all be spelt correctly for SPaG marks on this topic.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Bible is the primary Christian source of wisdom; 2 Timothy 3:16 (“God-breathed”) is the key text; Dei Verbum (Vatican II) teaches that Scripture and Tradition together form one deposit of revelation for Catholics. Christians interpret biblical authority as literal Word, inspired Word, or source of guidance.
  • The Church split into Catholic/Orthodox (Great Schism 1054, Filioque controversy) and Protestant (Reformation, Luther 1517); leadership includes laity, ministers, bishops and the pope (Ephesians 4:11–12); women’s ordination is accepted by Anglican and most Protestant churches, not by Catholic or Orthodox.
  • Forms of expression include paintings (Michelangelo, Catechism 2502), icons (Orthodox), sculpture, symbols (Cross — Ephesians 2:10–19; fish), drama (mystery plays, passion plays), CS Lewis’s literature (The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe; The Great Divorce), and music (Gregorian Chant, Graham Kendrick, Casting Crowns).

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which Christians use the Bible in their daily lives.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Reading the Bible during personal devotion (private worship).
- Hearing the Bible read in church services — liturgical churches follow a lectionary ensuring all Scripture is covered over time.
- Using the Bible as a source of guidance when making ethical decisions.
- Reading the Bible for comfort and strength in times of difficulty.
- Using the Bible in study groups, Bible classes or Sunday School.
Each point must be identifiably separate.

practice_questions.text: Describe the significance of the Cross as a Christian symbol.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- The Cross is the primary symbol of Christianity, representing the crucifixion of Jesus and the means of salvation.
- Ephesians 2:10-19 describes Christ reconciling people to God through the cross, 'destroying the barrier, the dividing wall of hostility.'
- Different denominations use the symbol differently: Catholic and Orthodox churches typically display a crucifix (cross with the figure of Christ); many Protestant churches display an empty cross, symbolising the resurrection.
- The Cross appears in churches, on jewellery, in art and in corporate logos as a universal marker of Christian identity.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians interpret the authority of the Bible in different ways.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The Bible was written by many human authors over centuries in different literary genres (poetry, law, history, prophecy, letters), which makes uniform literal interpretation problematic. A poem like Psalm 103 cannot be read the same way as a historical account in Acts; understanding the genre and context shapes interpretation. This leads many Christians to hold an 'inspired' rather than a strictly literal view of biblical authority.
- Christians disagree about the relationship between the Bible, Church Tradition and individual conscience. Protestant Christians, following sola scriptura, hold that the Bible alone is the final authority; Catholic teaching (Dei Verbum) places Scripture and Tradition alongside each other, with the Magisterium as the authentic interpreter. These different starting points produce different ways of weighing what the Bible says against what the Church has always taught.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why art, music or drama is important in Christian worship, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Visual art (paintings, icons, sculpture) helps Christians focus on the realities of faith that words alone cannot express: an icon of Christ or a painting of the Crucifixion draws the worshipper into contemplation of divine truths. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2502 says sacred art 'evokes and glorifies, in faith and adoration, the transcendent mystery of God.'
- Music deepens worship by engaging the emotions and memory: Gregorian Chant has been used in Catholic and monastic worship for over a thousand years, creating an atmosphere of prayer and reverence. Contemporary music by Graham Kendrick and Casting Crowns makes faith accessible to new generations, expressing belief in forms culturally relevant to today's worshippers.

The 5th mark: name a specific source — 'Catechism of the Catholic Church 2502', 'Ephesians 2:10-19 (the Cross)', 'Musicum Sacrum (1967 Vatican document on sacred music)', or a named artist/work. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The role of women in the Church should be equal to that of men in all Christian denominations.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- Romans 16:1-16 shows women in significant leadership roles in the early Church: Phoebe is called a diakonos (deacon), Priscilla is a co-worker in the Gospel, and Junia is described as 'outstanding among the apostles.' If women held these roles in the New Testament Church, the Church today should reflect this equality.
- The Church of England ordained women as priests in 1994 and as bishops from 2015; the Methodist Church has had women ministers since 1974. These denominations argue that the Gospel breaks down gender hierarchies ('neither male nor female... all one in Christ Jesus') and that the Kingdom of God is characterised by equality.
- Limiting women's leadership roles restricts the exercise of the gifts the Holy Spirit gives to all believers (1 Corinthians 12). The Body of Christ needs all its members functioning to capacity.

Arguments against:
- The Roman Catholic Church teaches that its inability to ordain women to the priesthood is a definitive teaching: Christ chose twelve male apostles and the Church has no authority to change this. This is not presented as a cultural preference but a theological conviction about the nature of the priesthood.
- 1 Corinthians 14:33-40 has been interpreted by many evangelical and Catholic Christians as indicating that authoritative teaching in the assembly is a male role. Some argue this reflects a created-order principle that transcends cultural context.
- Some Christians argue that equal dignity does not require identical roles: men and women can have complementary roles of equal value. The Catholic and Orthodox traditions affirm women as essential to the life of the Church while reserving the ordained priesthood to men.

SPaG: 'denomination', 'conscience', 'Reformation', 'Filioque', 'ordination' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which CS Lewis's writing expresses Christian belief.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950) uses allegory to communicate the Christian doctrine of atonement and resurrection: Aslan (representing Christ) allows himself to be killed by the White Witch (representing evil and sin) and returns to life, breaking the 'deep magic from the dawn of time.' Readers engage with the themes of sacrifice, redemption and resurrection through a fantasy narrative rather than a theological treatise — making the ideas accessible to children and adults unfamiliar with Christian doctrine.
- The Great Divorce (1945) explores the nature of heaven and hell through an allegorical journey, presenting heaven as fully real and earth as merely 'the shadow-lands.' Lewis argues that people who reject heaven do so by clinging to petty selfishness — they choose themselves over God. This expresses the Christian teaching that hell is ultimately self-chosen separation from God rather than external punishment.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

glossary_terms.definition: The Christian sacred scripture, consisting of the Old Testament (Hebrew scriptures) and the New Testament (writings about Jesus and the early Church).
A Vatican II document (1965) on divine revelation — it describes Scripture and Tradition as two channels of God's one divine revelation, both entrusted to the Church.
The separation of the Western (Catholic) and Eastern (Orthodox) Church in 1054, largely over the Filioque dispute and papal authority.
The 16th-century movement, led by figures such as Martin Luther and John Calvin, that challenged Catholic authority and gave rise to Protestant Christianity.
Latin meaning 'and the Son' — the clause added by Western churches to the Nicene Creed, stating the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father AND the Son. Rejected by Eastern Orthodox churches.
Paul's image in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12 of the Church as a single body with many different members, each contributing different gifts.
Three-dimensional sacred images — including statues of Jesus, Mary and the saints — used in Catholic and Orthodox worship as aids to devotion.
The authors of the four Gospels — Matthew (a man/angel), Mark (a lion), Luke (an ox) and John (an eagle) — represented by traditional symbols in Christian art.
Medieval dramatic performances depicting scenes from biblical history, staged by craft guilds at festivals.
Dramatic performances depicting the events of Jesus's Passion and crucifixion, notably the Oberammergau Passion Play performed every ten years in Bavaria.
